items.title: Lithium reacts less vigorously than sodium even though it is above it
items.claim: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs all react more violently with water in turn. Yet lithium has the highest ionisation energy AND the most negative standard electrode potential (-3.04 V — even more negative than caesium's -3.03 V).

options.text: Lithium is mislabelled — it should be in Group 2
Reactivity with water is rate-controlled by surface kinetics: lithium has a high melting point and forms a thick LiOH crust, so it reacts slowly even though it is highly thermodynamically active
Lithium doesn't really react with water at all
The standard electrode potential table is wrong

items.reveal:
Standard electrode potential measures the thermodynamic tendency to release electrons in aqueous solution. Lithium's small ion has very high hydration enthalpy (-519 kJ/mol vs caesium's -264), which more than compensates its higher ionisation energy.

But observed reactivity also depends on how fast the metal can deliver electrons. Lithium has a higher melting point (181°C) than sodium (98°C), so it does not melt in the heat of its own reaction with water. The LiOH product is less soluble than NaOH and forms an adherent coating. So lithium fizzes calmly; sodium spits and ignites.

Down the group, melting points drop, hydroxides become more soluble, and surface kinetics dominate.
items.why: Reactivity series is often presented as a single ladder. Real reactivity needs both thermodynamic driving force AND a kinetic pathway.

items.title: Frost forms by water vapour skipping the liquid state entirely
items.claim: Water vapour in cold air can deposit directly onto a windowpane as ice crystals without ever becoming liquid. The reverse — solid to gas without melting — is called sublimation, and is how freeze-drying works.
items.prompt: Why does water sometimes skip the liquid stage?

options.text: Water bends the laws of phase transitions
At pressures below the triple point (6.1 mbar for water) the liquid phase is not stable — water can only exist as solid or vapour, and transitions go directly between them
Frost forms only from existing ice
Liquid water is too dense for cold air

items.reveal_title: Below the triple point, liquid disappears
items.reveal:
Water's triple point sits at 0.01°C and 6.1 millibar — the only temperature and pressure where solid, liquid and vapour coexist. Below this pressure the liquid phase is unstable; water can only be vapour or ice, and crossing the boundary means sublimation or deposition.

At atmospheric pressure (1013 mbar) water can be liquid between 0 and 100°C, but small pockets of supercooled vapour near a cold surface can deposit straight to solid because the local equilibrium prefers ice over the metastable liquid intermediate.

Freeze-drying exploits this: freeze food, lower the pressure below the triple point, and the ice sublimes away with no melting. The structure is preserved, water is removed, and the result is light, stable food (instant coffee, astronaut meals, pharmaceutical formulations).
items.why: Solid to gas skipping liquid is treated as a curiosity. It is the dominant transition at low pressure and underpins multibillion-dollar industries.

items.title: Rubber heats up when stretched, cools when relaxed
items.claim: Stretch a rubber band quickly and press it to your lip — it feels warm. Let it snap back and it feels cool. Stretching does work ON the rubber, but the rubber gives heat OUT.
items.prompt: Why does stretching rubber release heat?

options.text: Stretching aligns the polymer chains, dramatically reducing entropy — the system must release heat to keep delta G zero at constant T and constant tension
The rubber band's atoms vibrate faster when stretched
The rubber compresses internally as you stretch it externally

items.reveal:
Most materials store elastic energy in bond stretching (enthalpy). Rubber stores almost no energy in bonds — its restoring force comes from entropy.

Unstretched rubber chains are tangled and random (high entropy). Stretching forces them into more aligned configurations (lower entropy). To keep free energy minimised at constant temperature, the system releases heat to the surroundings.

The consequence (Gough-Joule effect): a stretched rubber band CONTRACTS when heated, the opposite of steel. Heat the band and you increase tension on its disordered state — pulling it more tightly random.
items.why: Most students associate stretching with stored energy in bonds. Rubber's elasticity is statistical mechanics, not chemistry.
